Periodic Table of Elements. An organized arrangement of all known chemical elements in rows and columns, reflecting their atomic structure and chemical behavior. Developed principally by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, it has become the foundational reference tool in chemistry, organizing elements by atomic number and revealing deep patterns in their properties and reactivity.

It arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number—the number of protons. Elements in the same column share similar chemical properties due to identical electron configurations in their outermost shell. Divided into periods, the horizontal rows, and groups, the vertical columns, elements in the same group exhibit remarkably similar reactivity and bonding patterns across multiple chemical reactions.

Mendeleev's genius was not only organizing known elements but predicting unknown ones by leaving gaps in his table. Subsequent discoveries confirmed his predictions with astonishing accuracy. The table reveals the periodicity of chemical properties. As atomic number increases, chemical behavior repeats in a cyclical pattern, reflecting the filling of electron shells. It separates elements into categories—metals, nonmetals, and metalloids—and further subdivides them into families like alkali metals, halogens, and noble gases, with shared characteristics.

The table visually encodes quantum mechanical principles. Period number equals the number of electron shells, and group number relates to valence electrons in most main-group elements. Modern periodic tables include synthetic elements created artificially, extending far beyond the sixty-three elements known in Mendeleev's time. The heaviest elements are unstable and radioactive, pushing the boundaries of nuclear physics and chemistry.
